summary:
Kogi State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reaches far beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

The Criminal Code applicable in Kogi separately criminalises sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years. Kogi is not one of the twelve Shari'a-administering northern states, so the federal 14-year maximum governs there and the death penalty does not apply; those twelve states impose harsher penalties, and the encyclopedia entry records death penalties applied in Kano and Katsina for lesbianism.

Sexual orientation carries criminal exposure at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Shari'a law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

In 2022 a coalition of Nigerian human rights organisations won a court ruling that Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Act breached the Constitution and could not be enforced anywhere in the country, which in practice has allowed LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals to exist and organise. The same source records no comparable ruling for the conduct and marriage-prohibition provisions, so those remain enforceable, including in Kogi.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people. The Constitution contains no specific protections on the basis of sexual orientation, and there are no national anti-discrimination protections covering LGBTQ people.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's updated travel advice for Nigeria, reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, of death-penalty risk under Shari'a law in some northern states, and notes that the Same Sex Marriage Prohibition Act reaches helpers and attendees of same-sex weddings.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama was found on a highway in Abuja; police opened an investigation, and she had been stabbed a year earlier and had feared for her life. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common across Nigeria, including in Kogi, and are especially frequent in northern states. Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment: the Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

The most prominent case of trans-specific imprisonment concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), who pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison would hold her, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to official discretion, and an October 2024 investigative panel found that housing her in a maximum-security facility violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
The penalty gap between Kogi and the Shari'a-administering states is the sharpest comparative fact for a visitor routing through the country: Kogi carries the national 14-year maximum, while twelve northern states add religious-law provisions under which male sodomy can attract the death penalty. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office has built that distinction into its travel warning, which separates the secular sentence from the northern death-penalty risk.

Enforcement intensity varies by geography more than by statute. Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are reported as common nationwide and especially frequent in the north, which means that a state whose own statute is less severe can still see the national Act applied through police action.

The 2022 constitutional ruling sits alongside, rather than against, the Act. By voiding the organisational and association clauses while leaving the conduct and marriage provisions intact, it has produced a situation in which LGBTQ+ groups can operate with some legal footing while the underlying sexual-conduct offences remain live.

Two parallel risks operate outside the courts. One is police discretion, illustrated by documented beatings and extortion of men stopped for looking gay. The other is organised extortion by kito gangs using dating apps, which does not require any state actor and targets visitors who arrange meetings.

Official language in death investigations has been contested: police described the killed transgender woman as a man in female clothing, and press coverage of the Bobrisky sentence questioned openly which prison should hold a crossdresser. Both point to administrative practice, not statute, deciding how a trans person is treated in custody.
localsOnly:
Nigerian citizens and residents live under a statute whose association and public-display clauses have been held unconstitutional, giving LGBTQ+ organisations a basis to register and convene, while the sex and marriage offences remain on the books and enforceable.

There is no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the Constitution offers none either. Redress for a Kogi resident therefore depends on general criminal-law and human-rights remedies rather than on any equality provision.

Correctional placement for a trans person is governed by legislation rather than by identity documents alone. The October 2024 panel finding that maximum-security placement breached the Nigerian Correctional Service Act for a first-time offender is the clearest published constraint on how the authorities may house a transgender prisoner.

Residents of Kogi share the exposure recorded in other non-Shari'a states: the national 14-year maximum applies, the police retain the power to arrest under the Act, and the practical deterrent effect of the law is described by those affected as a climate of hostility independent of the statutory text.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing reported in 2022 have been enacted is unresolved in the sources assembled here, and no Kogi-specific legislative instrument on gender expression is sourced.

No Kogi-specific enforcement data, arrest figures or state-level police directives are sourced. The finding that mass arrests occur in Kogi rests on national reporting rather than on state records, and its frequency relative to other states is not established.

The practical reach of the 2022 ruling after judgment is not sourced: whether Kogi police and prosecutors have adjusted practice in response, and whether any appellate review followed, remain unresolved.

The Human Rights Watch Nigeria country page supplied for this pass yielded no additional finding beyond the October 2016 material already cited, so any post-2016 changes to police practice documented by that organisation are not covered here.

It is not sourced whether a transgender visitor to Kogi would be admitted under a passport or identity document that does not match presentation at immigration or security screening; no entry-document rule specific to trans travellers appears in these sources.
